<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par154 />are actually co-ordinate. Frequently the language employs merely the simple connexion by {{GHGterm|Wāw}}, even to introduce an antithesis ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=2|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=25}}, and very frequently in circumstantial noun-clauses), or when one of the two clauses is not co-ordinated, but subordinated to the other. On the use of {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} to introduce circumstantial clauses, cf. especially {{GHGpar|141|e}} and {{GHGpar|142|d}}; introducing causal clauses, {{GHGpar|158|a}}; comparative clauses, {{GHGpar|161|a}}; final clauses, {{GHGpar|165|a}}; consecutive clauses, {{GHGpar|166|a}}. On {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}, cf. {{GHGpar|143|d}}, and the sections there cited; on the use of {{GHGterm|Wāw}} in numerical sayings, cf. {{GHGpar|134|s}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|154|b}}
Rem. Sometimes wāw copulativum joins a sentence apparently to what immediately precedes, but in reality to a sentence which is suppressed and which must, therefore, be supplied from the context. So especially {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} with imperatives to express inferences, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=22}} {{GHGheb|text=וְשַֽׁאֲלִי|translate=ask now rather}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=18|verse=32}} ''for I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth''..., {{GHGheb|text=וְהָשִׁיבוּ|translate=wherefore turn yourselves}}. Also at the beginning of a speech in loose connexion with an act or speech of another person, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=4|verse=14}}, 41, 7:13, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=25|verse=9}}; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=7|verse=7}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְלוּ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=2|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=4|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=7}}. Sometimes the suppression of the protasis is due to passionate excitement or haste, which does not allow time for full expression; this is especially illustrated by {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=12|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=20|verse=3|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְלוּ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=22|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=28|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=22}} ({{GHGheb|text=וָלָ֫מָּה}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=1|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=7|verse=19|hidebook=1}} (cf. verse 2); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=2|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=2|verse=6}} (at the same time a circumstantial clause ''whereas I=and yet I have'', &c.); cf. also a new clause beginning with the formula of wishing {{GHGheb|text=וּמִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=29}}; on the disconnected use of {{GHGheb|text=וָלֹא}} and {{GHGheb|text=וָיֵשׁ}} cf. § 159 ''dd''.<section end=par154 />

<section begin=par155 />{{GHGpar-heading|155|Relative Clauses}}

<div style="font-size: small; text-align: center;">See V. Baumann, {{GHGcite|title=Hebräische Relativsätze}}, Leipzig, 1894 (cf. the heading of § 138 above); G. Bergsträsser, ‘Das hebr. Präfix {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}},’ ''ZATW.'' 1909, p. 40 ff.<ref>In this exhaustive article the author shows that between {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}} (on the pronunciation see § 36) and {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} there is syntactically no primary difference, but only a secondary distinction which arose in the course of the development of the language, namely that {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} is preferred in combinations which are customary in the old literary language, and {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}} in those which are derived from the popular language or from Aramaic.</ref></div>

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|a}}
'''1.''' By {{GHGpar|138|a}}, ''e'', relative clauses are divided into two classes: those which are used for the nearer definition of a noun (substantive or pronoun), and those which are not dependent on a noun. The former may be called ''incomplete'', the latter ''complete'' relative clauses.

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|b}}
Complete relative clauses, as a rule (see the exceptions under ''n''), are introduced by the originally demonstrative pronoun {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}; see further in {{GHGpar|138|e}}. Similarly, incomplete relative clauses may also be introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}, or by some other demonstrative pronoun; see further in {{GHGpar|138|a}} and ''g''–''k''. Very frequently, however, especially<section end=par155 /><noinclude>
